Windows 95, Windows 98, Windows 2000, Windows NT 4.0, and Terminal Server systems allow a remote attacker to cause a denial of service by sending a large number of identical fragmented IP packets, aka jolt2 or the "IP Fragment Reassembly" vulnerability.

### Impact

`stringify` and `uneval` serialize a typed array by emitting its backing `ArrayBuffer`, not just the view. In the case of a Node `Buffer` object, the backing buffer is a process-wide shared pool, meaning unrelated memory can be serialized into a response that is then sent to the client. For a Node `Buffer` the backing store is Node's **process-wide shared pool**, so serializing a small `Buffer` copies up to 64 KB of unrelated process memory — including bytes from other in-flight requests — into the output. In an SSR framework (SvelteKit, Nuxt) a public page whose `load()` returns a 2-byte `Buffer`, or a small file read with `readFileSync`, ships another user's request body / `Authorization` header in its HTML. Unauthenticated, silent, ~43,000× amplification.

This is serialization-side, so the `parse`/`unflatten` prototype-pollution and DoS guards do not apply — it fires on every SSR render, not only when parsing untrusted input.

### Workarounds

Convert Node `Buffer` objects to `Uint8Array`:

```diff
payload = {
- buffer
+ buffer: new Uint8Array(buffer)
}
```

cves.summary:
### Impact

The generated `activate` (bash/zsh) and `activate.fish` scripts interpolate a `shlex.quote`-ed value into a position that quotes it a second time. The extra quotes terminate the quoted run early and leave part of the value parsed as shell code, so a path containing shell metacharacters runs commands when a user sources the activation script.

`activate` is affected through the virtual environment's own path, on the branch that reports a relocated environment:

```sh
echo "Virtual environment directory __VIRTUAL_ENV__ does not exist!" >&2
```

For a destination named `x'$(id)'y`, `shlex.quote` emits `'x'"'"'$(id)'"'"'y'`. The inner `"` closes the enclosing double quote and `$(id)` is left unquoted. Backtick and `;` payloads reach the same result. This branch runs whenever the recorded path is absent, which is the normal case for a virtual environment copied or distributed to another machine.

`activate.fish` is affected through the interpreter's Tcl/Tk library paths:

```fish
set -gx TCL_LIBRARY '__TCL_LIBRARY__'
```

`shlex.quote` already returns `'/tcl/(cmd)/lib'`, so the rendered line is `''/tcl/(cmd)/lib''`. fish concatenates the adjacent quoted runs and expands the `(cmd)` left between them. The same doubling also splits a path containing a space into two list elements, corrupting `TCL_LIBRARY` and `TK_LIBRARY`.

This is the same defect class as GHSA-x78j-v8h9-3j2q, which covered `activate.bat`.

### Patches

Fixed in 21.7.13 by moving the placeholders outside the surrounding quotes, so each value keeps only the quoting `shlex.quote` applied. Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3252

### Workarounds

Avoid creating or distributing virtual environments whose path contains `'`, `` ` ``, `$`, `;`, `(` or `)`, and inspect the generated activation script before sourcing one you did not create.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

cves.summary:
`BatchActivator.quote()` returned its input unchanged, the only activator with no escaping at all. `--prompt`, the `VIRTUALENV_PROMPT` environment variable, and the config file all set the prompt, and `activate.bat` writes it straight into `@set "VAR=value"`. A prompt containing a double quote closes that string early, and whatever follows runs as live cmd.exe syntax:

```console
$ virtualenv --prompt 'x" & calc & "' venv
$ venv\Scripts\activate.bat
```

runs `calc` the moment someone activates the environment. Confirmed on a real Windows runner. Anyone who templates a prompt from untrusted input (a CI job using a branch name, a wrapper script deriving an environment name from user input) hands an attacker code execution in the shell of anyone who activates the resulting venv on Windows.

Fixed in 21.7.12 by escaping the characters cmd.exe treats as live syntax inside this construct. Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3250

When tarfile extracts a link on a system that doesn't support links, it falls back to extracting a member from the archive. In this case, the filter function is run twice: once for the extracted member, and once with name set to the location of the link. For one of the calls, the return value was ignored. Instead, the member should be skipped if either call returns None.

dcmjs, a JavaScript library for DICOM manipulation used in web-based medical
imaging viewers, contains an input validation bypass in its handling of DS
(Decimal String) and IS (Integer String) value representations.

The DecimalString and IntegerString classes in ValueRepresentation.js use a
regex sanitizer followed by JavaScript's Number() constructor. While the regex
strips direct NaN/Infinity strings, it preserves scientific notation (including
the 'e' character), enabling:

  1. Infinity injection via scientific notation overflow (1e999999)
  2. NaN injection via sign-only remnants from stripped inf strings ("-inf" -> "-")
  3. IS accepting scientific notation in violation of PS3.5

AFFECTED PRODUCT
================
Product:          dcmjs (JavaScript DICOM manipulation library)
Repository:       https://github.com/dcmjs-org/dcmjs
npm:              https://www.npmjs.com/package/dcmjs
Affected Versions: < 0.52.0 (patched in 0.52.0, released 2026-05-19)
CVE:              CVE-2026-46350 (assigned by GitHub 2026-05-13)
CWE:              CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation)
CVSS Score:       7.5 (HIGH)
CVSS Vector:      CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H
Maintainer note:  The CVSS score above is the reporter's assessment; dcmjs rates this low, because malformed input produces NaN/Infinity in values the caller must range-check in any case (both are reachable by other means, and no trust boundary enforced by dcmjs is crossed).

DOWNSTREAM IMPACT
=================
dcmjs is a foundational library used by:
  - OHIF Viewer (Open Health Imaging Foundation)
  - Cornerstone.js ecosystem
  - DICOMweb client/server implementations
  - Research and clinical web-based PACS viewers
  - Any Node.js or browser application parsing DICOM via dcmjs

ROOT CAUSE
==========
In src/ValueRepresentation.js, both DecimalString and IntegerString use:

    let returnVal = numberStr.trim().replace(/[^0-9.\\\-+e]/gi, "");
    return returnVal === "" ? null : Number(returnVal);

The regex /[^0-9.\\\-+e]/gi strips characters NOT in the set {0-9, ., \, -, +,
e, E}. This provides partial defense: direct "NaN" and "Infinity" strings are
stripped to empty/null. However:

  (a) Scientific notation is fully preserved because 'e', digits, '+', '-', '.'
      all pass the regex. "1e999999" passes intact, and Number("1e999999")
      returns JavaScript Infinity.

  (b) The string "-inf" is stripped to just "-" (only the minus passes the
      regex). Number("-") returns JavaScript NaN.

  (c) IntegerString uses the SAME regex/logic as DecimalString, meaning IS
      accepts scientific notation ("1e5" -> 100000) in violation of PS3.5
      Section 6.2, which restricts IS to characters 0-9, +, -.

  (d) No range validation exists for IS values (PS3.5 requires [-2^31, 2^31-1])
      or DS values (16-character max, fixed/floating-point only).

VULNERABILITY DETAILS
=====================

Attack Vector 1: Infinity via Scientific Notation Overflow
-------------------------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "1e999999"
Regex:   Passes (all chars in allowed set)
Result:  Number("1e999999") -> Infinity
Impact:  Infinity propagates through all downstream arithmetic

Attack Vector 2: Negative Infinity via Scientific Notation
-------------------------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "-1e999999"
Regex:   Passes
Result:  Number("-1e999999") -> -Infinity
Impact:  Negative Infinity in spatial/dosimetric calculations

Attack Vector 3: NaN via Sign-Only Remnant
---------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "-inf"
Regex:   Strips to "-"
Result:  Number("-") -> NaN
Impact:  NaN propagates silently through arithmetic (IEEE 754)

Attack Vector 4: NaN via Plus-Only Remnant
---------------------------------------
Input:   DS or IS field containing "+inf"
Regex:   Strips to "+"
Result:  Number("+") -> NaN
Impact:  Same as above

Attack Vector 5: IS Scientific Notation Bypass
--------------------------------------------
Input:   IS field containing "1e5"
Regex:   Passes
Result:  Number("1e5") -> 100000
Impact:  Integer fields accept non-integer representation, violating PS3.5

Attack Vector 6: IS Extreme Overflow
----------------------------------
Input:   IS field containing "1e18"
Regex:   Passes
Result:  Number("1e18") -> 1000000000000000000
Impact:  Far exceeds IS range [-2^31, 2^31-1], no bounds check

CLINICAL IMPACT
===============
dcmjs is used in web-based DICOM viewers and processing pipelines.
Corrupted values affect:

  - PixelSpacing / ImagePositionPatient: Spatial geometry corruption prevents
    accurate measurement and registration in web viewers

  - WindowCenter / WindowWidth: Display pipeline corruption makes images
    unreadable (all black or all white)

  - DoseGridScaling / NumberOfFrames: Radiation therapy dose display errors
    and denial of service via frame count overflow

  - RescaleSlope / RescaleIntercept: Hounsfield unit conversion produces
    invalid values, corrupting quantitative analysis

  - SliceThickness: Volume reconstruction fails in multiplanar reformats

# Security Vulnerability Report: Wails v2 — Origin Validator Bypass via Wildcard Pattern

| | |
|---|---|
| **Product** | wailsapp/wails (v2) |
| **Affected File** | `v2/internal/frontend/originvalidator/originValidator.go` |
| **Affected Versions** | All versions containing originValidator (latest as of 2026-03-26) |
| **CVSSv4.0** | **7.6 HIGH** — `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-625: Permissive Regular Expression |
| **Platforms** | Windows / Linux / macOS (all desktop targets) |

## Summary

Wails v2 provides `BindingsAllowedOrigins` to restrict which web origins can invoke Go backend methods via IPC. The wildcard pattern matching in `wildcardPatternToRegex` converts `*` to `.*` without anchoring subcomponents, allowing suffix-matched origins to bypass the restriction.

An attacker who controls a domain sharing a prefix with the allowed origin (e.g., `myapp.community` when `myapp.com*` is configured) can invoke arbitrary bound Go methods, potentially achieving file system access, data exfiltration, or code execution depending on the application's exposed API surface.

## Vulnerability Details

### Root Cause

`wildcardPatternToRegex` converts a wildcard pattern to a regular expression by escaping special characters and replacing `*` with `.*`. The substituted `.*` has no restriction — it matches any character sequence including dots and additional domain components.

### Vulnerable Code

**File:** `v2/internal/frontend/originvalidator/originValidator.go`

```go
func (v *OriginValidator) wildcardPatternToRegex(wildcardPattern string) string {
    specialChars := []string{"\\", ".", "+", "?", "^", "$", "{", "}", "(", ")", "|", "[", "]"}

    escaped := wildcardPattern
    for _, specialChar := range specialChars {
        escaped = strings.ReplaceAll(escaped, specialChar, "\\"+specialChar)
    }

    // * becomes .* — matches ANY character sequence, including dots and domain separators
    escaped = strings.ReplaceAll(escaped, "*", ".*")

    return "^" + escaped + "$"
}
```

The generated regex for `https://myapp.com*` is:

```
^https://myapp\.com.*$
```

This matches any string beginning with `https://myapp.com`, including:

- `https://myapp.community` — different TLD
- `https://myapp.com.attacker.com` — attacker-controlled subdomain
- `https://myapp.comXXXXX` — any arbitrary suffix

### Scope Note

The official comment in `options.go` gives `https://*.myapp.com` as the example pattern (subdomain prefix wildcard). This pattern is **not affected**. The vulnerability only manifests when developers use a trailing wildcard (`myapp.com*`), which is a natural misuse when intending to permit a domain and all its subpaths or ports.

## Impact

Any Go method registered with Wails bindings becomes callable from the attacker's origin. Depending on the application:

- File system read / write (common in desktop apps)
- Database queries
- OS command execution (if exposed via bindings)
- Sensitive configuration or credential access

## Fix

**PR:** https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/pull/5074

Wildcards are now only expanded when they represent a full domain component (immediately after `://`, `.`, or `:`). A wildcard appended to a partial label (e.g. `com*`) is stripped, preventing suffix-based bypasses. Comprehensive test suite added.

## Disclosure Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2026-03-26 | Vulnerability discovered during source code audit by @Saku0512 |
| 2026-03-26 | Private report submitted via GitHub Security Advisory |
| 2026-03-26 | Vendor acknowledgement and fix PR opened (#5074) |
| TBD | Patch release |
| TBD + 90 days | Public disclosure deadline |

### Summary A SQL Injection vulnerability exists in the Third Party (Company) update functionality of Dolibarr ERP/CRM. The `localtax1_value` parameter (`lt1`) is concatenated directly into an SQL UPDATE statement in `societe/class/societe.class.php` at line 1672 without any escaping, type casting, or parameterized query binding. An authenticated user with standard "Third Party: Create/Edit" permission can extract any data from the database, including password hashes, API keys, and all business data. Tested on Dolibarr v23.0.0 (latest stable), default installation via official Docker image, MariaDB 10.11. No custom modules, no modified configuration. ### Details **Vulnerable code** (`societe/class/societe.class.php`, line 1672): ```php $sql .= ",localtax1_value =".$this->localtax1_value; ``` The value comes from `GETPOST('lt1', 'alpha')` (`societe/card.php`, line 1135). The only sanitization applied is `trim()` at line 1528 — no `(float)` cast, no `$db->escape()`. The `alpha` input filter strips HTML tags and double quotes but does **not** strip single quotes, parentheses, commas, or SQL keywords. Since the injection point is in a numeric SQL context (no quotes around the value), the attacker needs none of the filtered characters. **Why the WAF does not block this:** Dolibarr's WAF (`waf.inc.php`) only checks SQL injection patterns in **GET** parameters, not POST. The POST-based `lt1` parameter bypasses it entirely. **The same vulnerability exists** for `localtax2_value` (parameter `lt2`) at line 1682. Adjacent fields like `localtax1_assuj` are properly cast to `(int)`, showing the developers were aware of injection risk but missed these fields. ### PoC **Steps to reproduce:** 1. Install Dolibarr v23.0.0 (tested with official Docker image, MariaDB 10.11) 2. Log in with a user that has "Third Parties: Create/Edit" permission (standard user, not admin) 3. Create or open any existing Third Party (company) record 4. Click "Edit" on the company card to open the update form 5. Intercept the POST request (e.g., Burp Suite) and add these parameters to the request body: - `localtax1assuj_value=1` - `lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)` 6. Submit the form (server responds with HTTP 302 Found — successful update) 7. Navigate to the company's Notes tab — the admin's MD5 password hash is now visible in the "Private Note" field **Verification:** `echo -n "admin123" | md5sum` → `0192023a7bbd73250516f069df18b500` (matches exfiltrated hash). **Figure 1 — Notes tab before exploitation (Private Note field is empty):** **Figure 2 — Burp Suite Repeater: full POST request headers and HTTP 302 Found response:** **Figure 3 — Burp Suite Repeater: request body with injected `localtax1assuj_value=1` and `lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)`:** **Figure 4 — Notes tab after exploitation: Private Note now contains `0192023a7bbd73250516f069df18b500` (MD5 hash of admin password "admin123"):** **curl PoC:** ```bash curl -b cookies.txt \ --data-urlencode "action=update" \ --data-urlencode "token=CSRF_TOKEN" \ --data-urlencode "socid=1" \ --data-urlencode "name=TestCompany" \ --data-urlencode "status=1" \ --data-urlencode "localtax1assuj_value=1" \ --data-urlencode "lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)" \ --data-urlencode "client=1" \ --data-urlencode "typent_id=0" \ "http://TARGET/societe/card.php?socid=1" ``` **Additional proof — arithmetic evaluation:** Sending `lt1=3+4` results in `localtax1_value=7.0000` stored in the database. The expression was evaluated by the SQL engine, confirming injection. **Additional proof — user count exfiltration:** Sending `lt1=(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM llx_user)` results in `localtax1_value=1.0000`. ### Impact An attacker with basic "Third Party: Create/Edit" permission (standard user, not admin) can: - **Read** any data from the database (password hashes, API keys, customer/supplier data, invoices, bank account details) - **Modify** any database record via additional SET clauses in the UPDATE injection - **Escalate** to admin by cracking MD5 password hashes (Dolibarr uses unsalted MD5 by default) - **Potentially achieve RCE** via admin features (Website module PHP injection, ModuleBuilder) after privilege escalation ### Suggested Fix ```php // societe.class.php, line 1528 — add (float) cast: $this->localtax1_value = (float) price2num(trim($this->localtax1_value)); // societe.class.php, line 1672 — add (float) cast: $sql .= ",localtax1_value =".((float) $this->localtax1_value); ``` Apply same fix for `localtax2_value` (lines 1529, 1682). ### Credit Please credit this finding to: **Grzegorz Tworek (F3715H) sec4check** (grzegorz.tworek@sec4check.pl) ### References A detailed write-up will be published after patch release at: https://www.sec4check.pl/blog/posts/cve-dolibarr-sql-injection-localtax-third-party.html We kindly request including this URL in the CVE references.

### Impact

An unauthenticated user could gain access to a server to execute arbitrary code on this server.

### Patches

This is fixed in the version 2.2.13. Users should upgrade to this version as soon as possible.

## Summary

In `backpropagate >= 1.1.0`, the optional Reflex web UI (`pip install backpropagate[ui]`, launched via `backprop ui`) exposes a training control plane: dataset upload, model load, training start/stop, multi-run orchestration, GGUF export, and HuggingFace Hub push.

The CLI accepts two operator-facing flags intended as security controls:

- `--auth user:pass` — documented as "require HTTP Basic authentication on every request to the UI."
- `--share` — documented as "expose the UI on a public address; requires `--auth`."

When `--auth user:pass` is passed, the CLI prints `Auth: enabled (user: <username>)` to confirm to the operator that authentication is active, then exports `BACKPROPAGATE_UI_AUTH=user:pass` to the subprocess that launches the Reflex backend.

**The Reflex backend (`backpropagate/ui_app/**`) never reads `BACKPROPAGATE_UI_AUTH`.** No authentication middleware is registered. No request-level guard runs. No WebSocket upgrade guard runs. Any client that reaches the bound port — local or remote, depending on whether `--share` is used — has full UI access.

An inline comment at `backpropagate/cli.py:1217-1218` in the v1.1.0 source documents the gap: *"For Phase 1 the variable is exported but Reflex doesn't read it yet."* This comment was internal-facing; the user-facing documentation (README, CHANGELOG, SHIP_GATE) advertised the contract as enforced.

This advisory is filed primarily because the runtime contradicted an operator-facing security claim. Code-only bugs of comparable shape (auth check missing entirely from a path) would already warrant disclosure; the additional false-promise dimension raises the severity.

## Impact

An attacker who reaches the bound port can:

- **Read uploaded datasets** rendered in the UI preview, including content of any JSONL/CSV/TXT file the legitimate operator has uploaded for fine-tuning.
- **Trigger arbitrary training runs** against any base model the operator has installed locally or that can be downloaded from HuggingFace.
- **Trigger HuggingFace Hub pushes** to repositories named via the UI input (subject to the operator's local HF token's scope — typically all repos owned by the operator).
- **Cause disk-fill DoS** via the `rx.upload` endpoint (no size cap, no extension filter, no per-session count cap in v1.1.0 / v1.1.1).
- **Read model paths** (`source_model_path`, `dataset_path`, `model`, `uploaded_path`) which are user-supplied and bypass the `safe_path()` helper that lives in `backpropagate/ui_security.py` (path validation is dead code on the Reflex surface in v1.1.0 / v1.1.1).

The combination of unauthenticated training control, HF push target spoofing, and path-input traversal makes the affected endpoint suitable for both data exfiltration (reading uploaded training data) and supply-chain attacks (pushing tampered model weights to the operator's HF account).

The local-only default (no `--share`) reduces exposure to a host-local attacker. The `--share` flag is documented as a "public URL" feature; operators who used `--share --auth user:pass` had no warning that the auth half was inert.

## Patches

Fixed in **v1.2.0** (released 2026-05-23). The patch implements real ASGI middleware via `rx.App(api_transformer=basic_auth_transformer)` that gates HTTP routes AND the `/_event` WebSocket upgrade. Four modes (`no_auth_local_only` / `token_auto` / `explicit_creds` / `production`), HMAC-signed cookie validated PRE-`websocket.accept()`, Host + Origin allowlists. The middleware ships alongside a 4-layer defense in depth at the cli.py / ui_app/app.py / rxconfig.py / env-strip surfaces so direct `python -m reflex run` invocations (bypassing the CLI guard) also enforce authentication.

Upgrade with:

- pip: `pip install --upgrade backpropagate`
- npm: `npm install -g @mcptoolshop/backpropagate@latest`

## Workarounds

If users cannot upgrade immediately:

1. **Do not pass `--auth` or `--share` to `backprop ui`.** Run the UI with no flags (`backprop ui`); it will bind to `localhost` and accept any client that can reach `127.0.0.1`.
2. **For remote access, use SSH port-forwarding** instead of `--share`:
   ```
   # On the client:
   ssh -L 7860:localhost:7860 <training-host>
   # On the server:
   backprop ui            # no --share
   # Then open http://localhost:7860 in your local browser.
   ```
   SSH provides the authentication layer the Reflex UI did not.
3. **Audit existing deployments.** If any host running `backpropagate >= 1.1.0` has previously been launched with `--share`, treat any uploaded training data, model paths, or HF push targets visible in that UI session as potentially exposed. Re-issue HF tokens that have been in use during such sessions.

**Binary distribution gap.** Standalone binaries (Windows .exe / macOS .app via PyInstaller) failed to build for v1.2.0 and will land in a follow-up patch release. In the interim, users who relied on the v1.1.x binary distribution should install the patched version via `pip install backpropagate==1.2.0` to receive the auth-bypass fix. The v1.2.0 PyPI package and `@mcptoolshop/backpropagate@1.2.0` npm package both carry the patched code.

In rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45, application data that a client buffers before the handshake completes is sent to the server even when the server rejects Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).

When the server rejects ECH, the client completes the handshake with the outer ClientHello and authenticates the server against the ECH config's `public_name`. At the end of the handshake, `start_traffic()` encrypts and queues any plaintext buffered by `ClientConnection::writer()`. It does this *before* checking for `EchStatus::Rejected` and queueing the `ech_required` alert.

The application then receives `Error::PeerIncompatible(ServerRejectedEncryptedClientHello)`, as expected. However, the client is still expected to call `write_tls()` to send the fatal alert, and that call also sends the encrypted application data. The server decrypts the data and only then receives the alert.

The ordering bug is older than 0.23.44. Before 0.23.44, the client checked the server certificate against the inner server name rather than `public_name`, so a correctly configured server failed certificate verification first and no data was sent. 0.23.44 fixed that check, which makes the ordinary rejection path reachable.

# Impact

Plaintext meant for the inner server, the one named in the encrypted ClientHello, goes to the client-facing server identified by `public_name`. That server is properly authenticated, so this is not an attack by an unauthenticated party. However this violates [RFC 9849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9849), which says the following:

- Section 6.1.6: if the handshake and authentication succeed after ECH rejection, the client "MUST ... abort the connection with an "ech_required" alert **before sending any application data to the server.**"
- Section 6.1.7: the certificate is checked only against `public_name`, and the connection "MUST NOT" be reported as successful to the application. rustls does report failure correctly. The problem is only that data is sent before the alert.

This affects only clients that meet all of these conditions:

- They use `EchMode::Enable`. GREASE ECH is not affected.
- They write application data before the handshake completes.
- They connect to a server that rejects their ECH config, for example because the config is stale. This is the same case where the server returns retry configs.

The usual client response to rejection is to retry with the server's retry configs. In that case, the data has already gone to the outer server.

## Summary

The client records the server-selected key-exchange group per server name when it processes the ServerHello, before the server is authenticated. A network attacker can answer one connection attempt for a target name with a ServerHello that selects X25519 and close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that name carry one X25519 share while supported_groups still lists X25519MLKEM768 first. If the server accepts that share instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only and no error.

An attacker that answers one connection attempt for the target name with a ServerHello selecting X25519 changes every later ClientHello of that client for that name, for as long as the entry stays in the store. No certificate or completed handshake is needed: it parses the ClientHello, sends the ServerHello, and closes.

TLS 1.3 transcript binding stops an on-path attacker from editing the ClientHello of one connection. It does not stop the attacker from steering the client's prediction state beforehand, because that state is written from an unauthenticated message.

## What does not trigger it

- Servers that send a HelloRetryRequest. The connection stays hybrid and costs one extra round trip.
- A client configuration with resumption disabled: nothing is stored.
- A different server name: the record is per name.

## Impact

If the genuine server picks the group for which a share is present, instead of sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake completes with classical key exchange only, between two peers that both support the hybrid group. No error is raised. The confidentiality of recorded sessions against a future quantum adversary is lost for those connections (harvest now, decrypt later). There is no key compromise and no authentication bypass.

Note that this behaviour is discussed at length in [draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations) so the actual security impact is largely down to a server policy decision.

### Summary

Formatting a client session value with Debug exposes its TLS 1.2 master secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK. A custom session store that logs these values can disclose keys to readers of the logs. Ordinary connection and built-in cache diagnostics remain redacted, and the session-store interface already warns that its values are sensitive.

### Details

Derived formatters traverse the session's secret-bearing fields. This conflicts with the project's explicit [key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

### Proof of concept

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations could leak secret data by using the provided `Tls12ClientSessionValue` or `Tls13ClientSessionValue` in a way that triggers its implementation of the `Debug` trait.

### Impact

Such store implementations could leak the master secret for the TLS connection.

### Summary

The built-in (but disabled by default) Brotli certificate decoder bounds the output buffer but accepts an input-selected history window. A header of five bytes can specify a 1 GiB window allocation. A peer can abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request. A client must enable Brotli and connect to the peer; a server must enable Brotli and request a client certificate. Neither direction requires a trusted attacker certificate.

### Details

rustls calls `BrotliDecompress` which enables Brotli's large-window extension. rustls applies a limit to certificates, but this applies to the decompressed result, and not to any internal allocations the process requires.

### Impact

Client applications that enable the `brotli` feature will be vulnerable to malicious servers. Server applications that enable the `brotli` feature and enable client authentication will be vulnerable to malicious clients.

Potential for denial of service due to memory exhaustion from peers sending malicious Brotli-encoded certificates, for applications that enable Brotli decompression.
